baselineRequirements.text: The first complete release uses one agent instance per Minecraft server process.

Every agent has a stable `server_id`. Authentication, authorization, audit events, storage, and protocol resources are scoped to that ID so a future host supervisor can expose multiple separately secured servers.
Windows and Linux are supported. Current development and testing is primarily on Windows.
An existing Minecraft server directory can be selected without moving it into a Vesta-owned directory.
`managed`: Vesta launches and supervises the Minecraft process and can provide complete lifecycle control, stdin console commands, stdout streaming, crash policy, and process metrics.

`existing`: Vesta uses an existing server directory. It can optionally become the process supervisor, or use available adapters such as the connector, RCON, log tailing, a Windows service, or systemd. Capabilities must accurately report what is and is not available; no feature may pretend to work when the process cannot be controlled safely.
Start-on-agent-start and restart-after-crash are separate, opt-in policies. Crash restart supports bounded exponential backoff, crash-loop detection, and suspension with a durable notification.

Agent, Java, server software, modpack, mod, and plugin updates never restart the Minecraft server or agent automatically. A restart is a separately authorized operation, even when update checking or download is automated.

Owners install one Vesta product. Internally it contains a management agent and a small process supervisor; the installer manages both and normally does not ask users to configure their connection. The optional Minecraft connector mod/plugin is a third component installed only on a compatible server with owner consent. Vanilla operation remains supported.

The agent owns network APIs, identity, policy, configuration, operations, and integrations. The supervisor owns the managed Minecraft process, stdin command delivery, output draining, the bounded live console buffer, and process exit events. It has no network listener and exposes permission-protected local IPC through Windows named pipes or Unix domain sockets.

IPC grants the agent process control but gives the in-game connector only a restricted capability channel. Merely running on the same host or possessing connector credentials never grants supervisor command or management access.

Minecraft continues running across an agent crash, approved agent update, or agent-only service stop. Start-on-agent-start checks the supervisor's existing process generation and never creates a duplicate launch. Full Vesta shutdown and Minecraft Stop are distinct, explicit operations.

After reconnecting, the agent reconciles process generation/identity, exit events, operation journals, active maintenance, save-suspension cleanup, and Minecraft log offsets before it resumes automation. Missed commands or non-idempotent workflow steps are never blindly replayed.

A supervisor update remains pending until Minecraft is stopped. The panel prompts for an approved restart: issue `stop`, observe actual process exit, activate the supervisor update, launch Minecraft through the new supervisor, and verify readiness. A failed stop or update leaves a visible pending/failed operation rather than silently force-killing or starting duplicate processes.

OS shutdown integration attempts graceful Minecraft stop within the platform's available service shutdown deadline. Setup reports/configures that deadline where supported; abrupt power loss cannot be made graceful by software.

If the supervisor crashes while Minecraft survives, the agent identifies the process using more than a PID (including start time and launch identity), tails game logs, and reports degraded control. It can use a configured connector, RCON, or existing service adapter where available; full stdin control may require an owner-approved Minecraft restart.

Adopting a running existing server does not terminate it. Vesta initially uses available monitoring/control adapters and offers full supervision on the next approved restart. An existing Windows service or systemd unit may remain the process owner through an explicitly selected adapter; support and permissions are capability-detected, not assumed.

The ordinary launch definition is an executable and argument array with an explicit working directory. It is passed directly to process creation without shell interpolation. Changing executable paths, JVM arguments that load code, or service targets is a trusted operational capability.

Advanced locally registered launch presets can run an existing `.bat`, `.ps1`, or shell script for servers with custom startup needs. Remote users can select approved presets and validated parameters; registration and script authoring occur locally. The normal installer does not require any script knowledge.

Existing-server onboarding prefers taking over startup seamlessly: inspect supported script patterns, detect the Java executable, arguments, working directory, and required setup, then offer an equivalent supervised launch on the next approved restart. Preserve the original script; never silently rewrite it, run it merely to discover settings, or discard required custom steps.

Arbitrary scripts cannot always be safely converted. Offer an approved custom startup preset or an existing-service adapter instead of forcing migration. Supervision must identify the actual Minecraft child and surface limitations for detached children or scripts with their own restart loops. Owner-approved takeover must not create competing process owners or duplicate restarts.

Readiness distinguishes `process_alive`, `starting`, `ready`, and `degraded`. It combines server-adapter console patterns, game-port probes, connector signals where available, and configurable timeouts. A live process or open port alone is insufficient proof that a world is ready to accept players.
The system is completely self-hostable and does not depend on Vesta accounts.
A launcher installation has a device keypair. Successful pairing issues a server-scoped device credential; raw long-lived bearer secrets are not the target design.
Device private keys are non-exportable through normal Vesta UI/API flows. Each device pairs independently and can be revoked independently.
Minecraft-authenticated access is associated with a Minecraft UUID and one or more paired devices.
Passcode-only access is associated with the paired device when no UUID has been proven.
Administrative authority is granted only through the local Vesta wrapper console/CLI. Minecraft OP, LuckPerms, plugins, mods, or in-game commands cannot grant agent administration.

In-game linking may prove a Minecraft UUID and grant only the role configured by the server owner, but it is not required for normal pack access and is not part of the administrative bootstrap path. Its remaining value is limited to optional identity linking and offline-mode/future integrations such as Discord.
Local recovery commands can create a new owner pairing and optionally revoke all existing administrative access.
The initial ownership flow uses a short-lived, single-use pairing code. Local launcher-guided onboarding and a headless installer/CLI flow should use the same underlying bootstrap protocol.
Pairing and invitation codes are rate-limited, single-use, and expire after a configurable interval with a ten-minute default.
Owner may revoke any device. Other remote roles may revoke only principals and devices strictly below their own delegation rank.

One server-local Vesta principal is the canonical identity. Device keys, Minecraft UUIDs, Discord identities, pack-password grants, roles, and SFTP credentials attach claims/capabilities to that principal instead of creating separate account databases.
Entering a pack password bootstraps a device-bound pack grant so the password is not repeatedly transmitted. Password rotation can revoke all grants derived from the previous password.
Discord OAuth links a Discord identity to an existing/new local principal; it does not create an independent administrative authority.
External SFTP clients require a protocol-specific SSH key or password, but the credential maps to the same Vesta principal and role.
Offline recovery material remains separate by design so access can be restored after all online device credentials are lost.
Access is explicitly granted by the server owner.
The target model uses named, per-action capabilities and server-local roles, not only cumulative numeric levels.
Authorization is checked for every request and resource. Loopback or LAN location alone does not grant remote API administration.

Destructive operations use a two-step prepare/confirm protocol. The normal UX may still be a simple launcher "Are you sure?" dialog, but the server must bind confirmation to the exact operation, actor, target, and short expiry.
Built-in roles are supplied for a safe initial setup, and owners can create custom roles from named capabilities.
Invitations are role-specific, short-lived, and single-use. An authorized administrator selects the role before generating the invitation code.

Remote delegation follows a strict role hierarchy and cannot grant equal or greater authority. Owner and Administrator grants are local wrapper-console operations only. Administrators may invite Maintainers and lower; Maintainers may invite Moderators and lower only when explicitly granted a delegation capability (their default role cannot manage roles). The same rule continues down the hierarchy. Custom roles carry an explicit delegation rank, but rank alone never permits granting capabilities or resource scopes the delegator does not possess or is forbidden to delegate.
Built-in roles are Owner, Administrator, Maintainer, Moderator, Viewer, and Pack User. Pack User is a limited server principal with pack access and a safe status view, not general management access.

The initial product assigns one primary role to a principal, plus optional per-principal capability overrides. The persistence and policy model uses role assignments rather than a single role column so multiple-role composition can be enabled later without migrating identity records.

Effective policy supports inherited role allowances and explicit principal or scoped denies. Explicit deny wins over inherited allow; an individual allow cannot bypass a hard security invariant or grant beyond the delegator's scope.

Role assignments and individual overrides may have an optional expiry. Expired authority stops applying immediately and produces a notification/audit event; permanent grants remain the ordinary default.

File capabilities can carry normalized path scopes and separate list, read, create, overwrite, rename, mkdir, and delete rights. For example, a role may edit `config/**`, read `logs/**`, and have no world access.
Owner has all server-local authority, including local recovery and granting Administrator, subject only to hard security invariants.

Administrator has broad remote operational, configuration, identity, integration, and pack authority, but cannot remotely create Owner or Administrator, invoke local recovery, erase protected security history, or bypass hard security rules.

Maintainer can manage lifecycle, raw console, files, content, backups, schedules/workflows, maintenance, and diagnostics by default. It cannot manage roles, credentials, security policy, owner recovery, or agent installation. These broad trusted-operator defaults are confirmed; owners may create narrower or more specialized custom roles by tweaking the capability presets.
Moderator defaults to player visibility and typed moderation actions. Raw console and unrestricted file access are disabled unless explicitly granted.

Viewer can see detailed server status, metrics, online player identities, activity history, and task progress without mutation rights. Logs and console output are separate opt-in capabilities because they may contain sensitive information.
Pack User receives pack access and the limited status surface only.

Permission to install executable mods/plugins, replace startup code, or alter code-loading JVM arguments is permission to execute code as the Minecraft OS identity. Raw console can also invoke powerful installed plugin commands. Vesta describes these capabilities as trusted-operator access, not as a contained or harmless form of file editing. Maintainer's current defaults imply that trust; a narrower custom role should be used for limited helpers.

The recommended service installation separates the Minecraft OS identity from the management agent's identity and protects agent state, vault keys, supervisor control IPC, update files, and locally approved script definitions with OS permissions. Merely hiding paths in the panel is not isolation.

Locally approved presets and launch scripts must not be editable through a lower-trust file capability. If their content changes, approval/hash validation is required before execution. Connector IPC cannot acquire agent-level powers.

Portable same-user operation remains possible, but clearly reports its weaker isolation: a malicious plugin may access anything that OS user can access. No API permission system can contain arbitrary code running as its own identity.

File scopes also govern archive creation/extraction, trash recovery, backup browsing/selective download, and exports; those routes cannot bypass a denied path. Full recovery exports and restoring backups remain owner-authorized.

Typed moderation actions validate identifiers and each argument using the selected server adapter; newlines/control characters and command interpolation cannot turn a limited action into extra raw-console commands.
Pack download authorization and server-management authorization are separate policy domains. Having permission to join or sync does not imply permission to administer the server.
Pack access supports at least `public`, `password`, and `minecraft-policy` policies.

`minecraft-policy` verifies the Minecraft UUID and evaluates the Minecraft server's real admission data rather than maintaining an unrelated Vesta list: whitelist state and `whitelist.json`, plus player bans where applicable.
A player does not need to run an in-game link command before receiving a pack; a player unable to obtain the pack may not be able to join and run that command.
Administrative roles are granted through local bootstrap/recovery or an explicit role-scoped device invitation.
Offline-mode servers cannot use Mojang-backed `minecraft-policy`. They may use password-gated pack access, or public pack download with only a limited public status view.

Microsoft/Minecraft authentication may still prove an online Minecraft UUID for device identity or explicitly granted management access when the Minecraft server itself runs in offline mode. That does not automatically make the UUID equivalent to an offline-mode player identity.

Offline-mode owners explicitly accept that Minecraft player identity is not cryptographically trustworthy. Vesta does not invent a stronger mapping or treat a linked online UUID as the joining offline player. Maintenance and admission use the server's actual whitelist data as-is, with future external authentication adapters left as a later extension.

If a UUID fails the server admission policy, including a banned player or a player absent from an enabled whitelist, it receives only the configured public/password fallback access rather than Minecraft-policy access.

Limited Pack User/public status contains server branding, online state, player count without player names, MOTD, Minecraft/loader version, pack name/version, and required-update state. It excludes detailed metrics, logs, identities, paths, software inventory, security configuration, and management data.
Pack state distinguishes the latest available revision from the minimum revision currently allowed to join.
The sync/status contract accepts the client's installed revision and reports one of `current`, `update_available`, or `update_required`.
The active status records the latest revision and minimum required revision so clients and operators can explain why an update is required.

New installations always receive the one currently hosted latest revision. An existing installation below latest but at or above minimum receives `update_available`; one below minimum receives `update_required`. Hosting only the latest does not invalidate an already installed still-allowed revision.

Owners may publish an optional pack, an optional update, or an immediately required update. There is no scheduled grace-period enforcement in the baseline because mismatched client/server mods frequently cannot interoperate.

Every Build/Publish increments revision. During publication the owner chooses whether minimum revision remains unchanged (optional update) or advances to the new revision (immediately required update).

Synchronization uses an internal automatically increasing integer revision. Pack presentation also has an owner-managed numeric/dotted display version. The owner increments that value manually; publishing a lower value is allowed only after an explicit warning because revision, not display ordering, remains the authoritative update signal.
Only the current published pack manifest and its files are hosted. Previous pack states are retained through the configured backup system rather than a public version-history API.

The editable pack workspace is a draft. Server-side mod changes never silently mutate it; Vesta calculates suggested additions, removals, and updates and marks the pack potentially outdated until an authorized user applies or dismisses them. Clients continue receiving the current published revision until a manual Build/Publish succeeds. The owner receives a persistent pending-publication or server/pack-mismatch notification while action is needed.

Build and Publish are one durable action: validate and display the complete release diff, generate optional release notes, build/sign in staging, increment the monotonic revision, and atomically activate the new result.

Hosted client-pack release is distinct from updating code in the Minecraft server process. A successful normal Build/Publish makes the complete new pack revision available immediately; it does not wait for Minecraft to restart.

Owners may optionally schedule when a new pack revision becomes available. Scheduled release freezes the approved built artifact/diff, keeps the current pack public until activation, and revalidates authority and expected current revision before the switch. A draft edit or another intervening release cannot silently substitute different content or change the approved minimum revision. Only the active revision is publicly hosted; scheduled staging is private and storage-bounded. Failed/incomplete builds never replace the active pack.
The release diff classifies additions, removals, version changes, stale suggestions, custom overrides, symbolic links, and server/pack mismatches.
Rollback restores a selected backup into staging, validates it, and publishes the restored state as a new monotonic revision.

Installing a modpack into the Minecraft server directory (not releasing its hosted client pack) uses the same transactional model as launcher instance updates: resolve and validate a complete plan, create the configured safety snapshot, stage downloads, verify hashes, journal application of the file set, persist the new revision, and retain rollback metadata. A multi-file server-directory change is not claimed to be one filesystem-atomic operation; locks and a recoverable journal protect intermediate states.

Pack possession and revision claims are compatibility signals, not a security boundary. The agent does not attempt forgeable client attestation, and the connector is not required to prove that a non-Vesta client has the pack.
The Minecraft server directory is live. File-manager, external filesystem, mod, plugin, and configuration changes apply to that directory immediately; there is no unpublished server-files draft.

File changes never trigger an automatic restart. The standard restart control remains available and Vesta exposes a low-pressure changed-since-start and restart-required status when it can determine one.

The managed updater stages verified mod/plugin/server-JAR replacements and removals while Minecraft runs, then applies them after actual process exit on the next approved restart. Ordinary direct file management remains live, with executable-file risk warnings. This is not a server-file publication workflow. Java may load classes/resources after startup; loaded code is not a guarantee that replacing a running JAR is safe. Hosted client-pack releases remain immediate unless the owner explicitly schedules their release.

A custom hosted modpack has its own Vesta-managed workspace outside the live Minecraft server directory. It is never generated by scanning or copying the server root. The workspace contains the pack manifest/state plus a dedicated overrides directory for custom configuration and files.

The manifest remains schema-compatible with the launcher's existing `VestaIndex`: format version, name/version, revision/minimum revision, Minecraft/loader identity, dependencies, and file entries containing path, size, hashes, environment rules, and source metadata. Additions use a versioned backward-compatible contract rather than a second Vesta format.

Platform content is represented primarily by immutable metadata references: provider, project ID, version/file ID, expected hash, filename, and required environment. Vesta does not duplicate Modrinth/CurseForge-hosted bytes inside the pack merely because the same artifact is installed on the server.

Each published revision records an exact provider version/file ID and expected content hash. Editing the draft to select another provider version is normal, but a published revision never resolves a mutable `latest` selector or accepts different bytes under the same identity.

When installing/updating a server mod whose trusted metadata declares a client or shared requirement, Vesta offers a suggested manifest change but does not apply it automatically. Server installation and pack editing/publication remain separate operations. Updating/removing a matching server artifact produces an outdated/stale pack suggestion; ambiguous metadata asks rather than guesses.

Client-only provider mods can be added directly to the pack manifest and are downloaded by the launcher; no copy is placed in the server `mods` directory. Client-only custom/private files are explicit overrides.
Custom uploaded content without an external immutable source may be placed in the pack overrides workspace through an explicit pack operation. It is not implicitly copied from the live server tree.

Custom packs use the Vesta Pack manifest model aligned with the launcher's persisted instance/modpack state. The hosted representation is a small JSON manifest plus an optional compressed overrides archive, each hashed and bound to the same monotonic pack revision.

The launcher downloads referenced Modrinth/CurseForge artifacts directly from their provider. Missing or withdrawn content fails with a clear affected-file error. A validated provider-byte cache is optional, opt-in, storage-bounded, and subject to provider redistribution terms.

For manual portability, canonical `.vestapack` export wraps the manifest, overrides archive, metadata, and signatures into one container. Import may continue accepting `.vpack` as a compatibility alias. Network sync serves the manifest and overrides archive directly rather than expanding thousands of individual hosted files.
One overrides archive is the baseline because custom content is expected to be small or absent. Archive splitting is deferred until measured pack sizes show a practical need.

Importing an existing launcher instance or Vesta pack into the workspace is a destructive replace operation: preview, exact confirmation, and movement of the previous workspace into configurable pack trash precede replacement.

Published manifest bytes and the overrides-archive hash are signed by the server identity and bound to server ID and revision. Paired launchers reject invalid signatures, hash mismatches, and revision rollback.

Executable permission is not a remotely supplied pack-manifest capability. Pack extraction uses safe platform defaults and cannot mark downloaded content executable merely because a manifest requests it.
The overrides workspace and imported Vesta packs may contain symbolic links. The versioned manifest records link path and target explicitly rather than silently treating a link as an ordinary file.

Pack build/import scans links without following targets outside the workspace. Absolute, cyclic, special-file, or sandbox-escaping targets are rejected; contained relative links may be preserved for a sandbox-capable launcher.

Connecting to a server pack and manually importing a `.vpack` or `.vestapack` containing links displays a specific warning and the affected paths before acceptance. The launcher must validate containment again at extraction time.
Symlink acceptance is remembered only for the exact signed pack revision. A later revision containing links requires a new warning/acceptance so link targets cannot change without the user noticing.

Pack metadata includes icon, description, author, optional changelog/release notes, recommended RAM, and optional support/homepage links. When release notes are omitted, Vesta proposes an editable summary generated from the release diff.

Optional client entries are a supported Vesta manifest capability, including a default enabled state and user selection before installation/update. More complex dependency groups, conflicts, and mutually exclusive choices may be phased after the basic optional-file implementation.
Pack builds occur only after an explicit authorized Build/Rebuild action; automatic, debounced, and scheduled rebuilds are outside the baseline.

`.vesta-packignore` applies only to the dedicated overrides workspace; `.vesta-fileignore` applies to HTTPS/SFTP visibility in the live server root; and `.vesta-backupignore` applies only to backup inclusion. Each uses documented gitignore-style semantics.
File-browser visibility defaults to hiding nothing in the Minecraft server tree except invariant protected Vesta state, credentials, keys, repositories, and other security-sensitive agent internals.

A build stages and verifies a complete manifest/archive pair, then atomically replaces the current published pair and increments the revision. The previous pack remains downloadable during the build; partial or mixed output is never exposed. Only the current revision is hosted after publication, with older pack workspace states available only through configured backups.
While building, Vesta-managed writes to the manifest and overrides workspace are rejected with a clear build-in-progress result. External mutation is detected and invalidates the build.
Owner and Administrator can manage, build, and publish packs by default.

Pack management uses dedicated capabilities so a custom Pack Maintainer role can edit the draft, manage provider references and overrides, build, publish, and inspect pack status without receiving live server-file or console access.

The Pack Maintainer preset may publish optional or required updates and raise `minimum_revision` by default. Owners can remove those capabilities or split edit/build/publish/force-update authority through custom role configuration.

Pack replacement/import uses ordinary pack-draft management authority plus the destructive-operation confirmation; it does not require a mandatory special role capability. Owners may still separate it through a custom deny/override.
Existing-server adoption and new-server installation.
Start, stop, restart, force kill, crash detection, and restart policy.
Live console, durable structured logs, and log search/download.
CPU, memory, disk, network, process, player, and tick-health monitoring where the selected process/connector mode supports them.
A constrained file manager and structured editors for known configuration.
Mod, plugin, modpack, server-JAR, Java runtime, and safe update workflows.
Player list, whitelist, OP, kick, ban, pardon, kill, and lightning-strike operations.
Backups, retention, integrity verification, restore, and recovery.
A durable scheduler owned by the agent.
Durable notifications that launchers can fetch after being offline.
Optional email, Discord, and generic webhook notification sinks.
Signed agent updates with automatic checks, explicit installation approval by default, staged activation, and rollback.
Update checks may run at startup and periodically, but update installation and any required restart remain explicit owner-authorized operations.

Graceful stop first sends Minecraft's normal `stop` command and enters a visible `stopping` state. The launcher Stop control may become a separately authorized Force Kill control while shutdown is pending; the timeout and unattended workflow behavior are configurable.

Crash restart has a configurable crash-loop breaker. The recommended preset is three failures within ten minutes, after which Vesta leaves Minecraft stopped, marks it unhealthy, and emits a critical notification.

Maintenance mode is a first-class state with a configurable reason/MOTD and an admission overlay for owners, administrators, and explicitly allowed players. It may reject new joins immediately, wait for non-maintenance players to leave, or remove them after a configured deadline before maintenance work starts.

Linked Minecraft UUIDs for Owners and Administrators are included in the recommended maintenance admission preset, with an additional explicit list of allowed maintenance players. Owners may configure a narrower policy.

The panel/API exposes the preserved normal whitelist and active temporary maintenance list as two distinct resources. Editing one never silently edits the other, and the UI explains which list applies after maintenance ends.

With a trusted connector, the admission overlay is enforced in-process without rewriting the normal Minecraft whitelist. Without a connector, Vesta snapshots the exact whitelist contents and enabled state, transactionally installs a temporary maintenance whitelist, reloads it, and journals restoration. Normal start after interrupted maintenance first restores or explicitly reconciles that saved state.

Entering and leaving maintenance are workflow-backed transitions. Owners may compose permitted pre-maintenance and post-maintenance actions, notifications, delays, scripts from local presets, backup, player countdown, kick policy, and the main maintenance operation without remotely uploading arbitrary code.
A failed pre-maintenance action aborts entry by default and reports the failed step. An Owner may explicitly continue or configure failure behavior for actions that are safe to ignore.

Optional sleep mode gracefully stops Minecraft after a configurable period with zero players, while the Vesta agent remains online. The public API and launcher distinguish `sleeping`, `waking`, `starting`, `maintenance`, `crash_loop`, `recovery_required`, and ordinary `offline` states.

While sleeping or otherwise intentionally offline, a lightweight Java Edition status responder may temporarily own the Minecraft TCP port. It returns a configurable protocol-compatible status/MOTD and can trigger a queued start on a login connection. Server-list status pings never wake Minecraft.

A login connection that triggers wake receives a configurable disconnect response such as "Server is starting; reconnect shortly." Vesta does not claim that the original login session can be transparently transferred to a process that has not started.
Concurrent or repeated login attempts coalesce onto one durable start operation and are rate-limited per source address. They cannot create parallel launches or bypass a start cooldown.

Before Minecraft starts, the status responder closes and releases the game port; readiness requires successful process bind and status probing. When the actual server is online it owns the port and its normal status response unless a future always-on proxy mode is explicitly enabled.

Wake behavior reports compatibility limitations for CGNAT tunnels, TCP forwarding services, modded handshakes, multiple game ports, and status bots. Status monitoring remains available without waking the process. Any compatible login attempt may request wake; authorization is still enforced by Minecraft after startup because the temporary responder cannot securely authenticate a UUID.

Vesta does not place an always-on proxy in front of a running server in the baseline. The temporary responder cannot transparently transfer the triggering login connection and does not intercept live traffic.

Automatic sleep performs a configurable in-game warning/countdown, is cancelled if a player joins, and is deferred while incompatible backup, update, maintenance, restore, or file operations are active.
Once the crash-loop breaker activates, network wake attempts return the configured unhealthy status/message but cannot start Minecraft until an authorized user clears the condition.

Without a connector, server-type/version-specific console parsers maintain the observed online-player set from join, leave, kick, and shutdown events. Vesta reconciles that set after startup and whenever evidence is incomplete so a missed line cannot incorrectly trigger sleep.

Status configuration distinguishes an online/live MOTD from offline-state templates. Templates exist for sleeping, waking, starting, maintenance, stopping, crash loop, recovery required, and ordinary offline states.

Templates support documented safe placeholders such as server name, current state, player counts, Minecraft/loader version, maintenance reason, queued operation, elapsed state time, estimated readiness when known, and a concise public-safe failure code. Secret paths, exception text, and administrative detail are never available as public placeholders.
The editor provides a two-line visual preview, Minecraft color/style controls, placeholder insertion and preview values, protocol-limit validation, and an authorized raw-text mode.
Owners may configure a normal icon and state-specific icons for offline, sleeping, starting, maintenance, and unhealthy/failure responses, with a generated fallback when a selected asset is invalid.
Offline-state status defaults to a truthful `0/0` player display. Maximum players and displayed version text may be configured per state, but Vesta does not fabricate named or nonzero online players.
The structured server-settings editor manages the ordinary live MOTD in `server.properties`, reports its reload/restart behavior, and preserves raw editing access for authorized users.

Vesta uses a safe server-specific reload only when the implementation proves one is supported. It does not invoke broad plugin reload commands merely to refresh an MOTD; otherwise the setting is marked Minecraft-restart-required.

When a compatible connector is installed, it may implement dynamic online status-ping/MOTD responses without rewriting `server.properties`. Without a connector, the actual running server owns its live status response and Vesta does not claim it can override that response dynamically.
The launcher/app status uses the same canonical lifecycle state and template inputs as the game-port responder, while presenting authorized diagnostic details separately from public MOTD text.
The remote file view covers the Minecraft server root but permanently hides agent internal state, credentials, private keys, update state, and backup storage.

Deletes and overwrites are recoverable by default through a quota- and retention-bounded trash system. Operations preflight required disk space and never silently consume the server's remaining capacity.
Trash uses both an absolute and percentage ceiling, with the lower limit winning. The initial recommended defaults are 10 GB, 10 percent of the volume, and seven-day retention; all are configurable.
Supported content origins include Modrinth, CurseForge, launcher uploads, local files, and explicitly authorized arbitrary URLs.

Hash verification is mandatory for arbitrary URL content. URL fetching also requires SSRF defenses, scheme/redirect restrictions, size limits, and clear unverified-origin labeling; a checksum proves byte identity, not trustworthiness.
Hashless arbitrary URL downloads are refused.
Mod and plugin changes are explicit manual operations. Replaced artifacts use recoverable file transactions/trash rather than creating a full server backup for every individual change.
Modpack updates recommend or create a safety snapshot according to backup policy because they can change a large coordinated file set.

Text reads return a content revision/hash. Edits use optimistic concurrency (`If-Match`-style) and reject stale writes with enough metadata to compare and deliberately retry, preventing one administrator from silently overwriting a newer edit.
Large HTTPS/launcher uploads are resumable, chunked, and verified per chunk and as a completed object. Interrupted upload staging is quota-bound and expires automatically.

Upload, download, extraction, archive, staging, and concurrent-operation limits start from secure presets calculated against available storage and host resources, with explicit owner-configurable ceilings and hard safety reserves.
Storage targets include local disk, mounted paths/NAS, and S3-compatible object storage.

The portable online-backup baseline coordinates Minecraft writes with version-supported save suspension and acknowledged flush (normally `save-off` followed by `save-all flush`), keeps autosave disabled while the backup engine reads the server tree, and restores its previous state on completion, failure, or cancellation using the crash-safety contract below. This trades minutes of world-save latency for a stable flushed Minecraft world without requiring temporary space equal to the server size.

`save-off` does not freeze every file in the server directory: logs and some plugins/mods may continue writing independent data. Without a filesystem snapshot or plugin-specific quiesce adapter, Vesta describes the world as save-consistent and the remaining live files as best-effort rather than claiming the entire directory is transactionally frozen.
Online backup may issue configurable advance and start notifications to the server console, players, launcher inbox, and external notification routes.
The recommended pre-backup player warning is 60 seconds. Its duration, messages, destinations, countdown cadence, and whether an authorized manual backup may skip it are configurable.

For the duration of a backup scan, Vesta rejects conflicting HTTPS file API, SFTP, pack-build, content-update, and other Vesta-managed mutations. Direct OS access and independent plugin/mod/log writes cannot be safely blocked without stopping the process; Vesta detects observable source mutations and records them in the backup result.

Source-mutation handling is configurable per backup profile: finish with a warning, fail when protected/important paths change, or fail on any detected mutation. The safe preset fails on world-data mutation and warns for known volatile logs/cache.

Mutation detection is best-effort, not proof that independent writes never occurred. A point-in-time filesystem view still requires writer coordination for plugin/application consistency; otherwise its result is crash-consistent.

An advanced optional write guard may temporarily deny the managed Minecraft OS identity new writes to configured paths and restore permissions from a durable journal afterward. It is disabled by default because existing open handles may remain writable and denied writes can break plugins/mods or lose their pending data. Vesta tests the guard, excludes required writable paths, warns players, and never labels this mechanism alone as a guaranteed filesystem freeze.

The write guard is configured per path and leaves Minecraft/agent logs and required runtime/temp paths writable in its recommended preset. If original permissions cannot be restored exactly, Vesta enters recovery-required state and blocks Minecraft launch until locally repaired or explicitly reconciled.
Backup inclusion supports a separate gitignore-style `.vesta-backupignore`. It is independent from hosted-pack and file-browser visibility policy.

Vesta separately detects optional point-in-time filesystem facilities such as Windows VSS, Btrfs, ZFS, or LVM. Here, "filesystem snapshot" means a temporary frozen source view, not a dated Vesta backup. When available and enabled, Vesta may hold `save-off` only through flush and snapshot creation, restore `save-on`, and let the backup engine read the temporary snapshot while play continues.

Filesystem-snapshot acceleration is configurable and never required. Vesta owns no new filesystem or volume format and falls back to the portable save-suspension flow when support or privileges are unavailable.
Temporary filesystem snapshots are read-only backup sources and are deleted after use. They are never automatically restored and do not alter the owner's dated Vesta backup history.
Stopped-server backup is the universal safe fallback.
Backup manifests include checksums and sufficient metadata for verification before restore.
Backup creation and automated backup schedules are opt-in. The agent may recommend a safety backup before risky changes but does not silently enable a recurring backup policy.
Incremental, deduplicated snapshots are the target design, with configurable retention and storage quotas.

With restic, all backup repositories are encrypted and authenticated, including local disk and NAS; it has no unencrypted repository mode. Setup generates a repository secret, stores it in the protected agent vault, and guides the owner to preserve a recovery copy. This does not require another everyday login. An owner-chosen repository passphrase is an advanced alternative. A separately authorized plaintext file export is not an unencrypted restic backup.
Restore supports full in-place replacement, selective paths, and restoration into a separate inspection directory.

No failure, crash loop, failed update, failed health check, or startup error automatically restores a backup. Restoration always requires an authorized owner decision and exact-operation confirmation.

Full restore always stops the Minecraft process. Before destructive restore, Vesta creates a pre-restore safety snapshot when storage permits; proceeding without one requires an explicit owner override.

Vesta orchestrates a bundled, signed mature backup engine such as restic for content-defined deduplication, authenticated encryption, repository integrity, and cross-platform storage support instead of implementing new backup cryptography.

Backup history, maximum count, maximum repository size, retention periods, and dated restore points are independently configurable regardless of whether a temporary filesystem snapshot was used to create them.

Repository-size limits are storage budgets with capacity preflight and a working-space reserve, not a promise that every incremental backup or prune can fit under an exact hard limit. Cleanup never silently deletes unexpired restore points to satisfy that budget.

Online backup requires an adapter capable of reliable save commands and flush acknowledgement. Exact commands vary by Minecraft/server version; unsupported variants use a compatible adapter or the stopped-server fallback.

A normal finally/cancellation handler is insufficient after an agent crash. Before save suspension, the supervisor records a bounded save lease tied to that exact Minecraft process generation. Expiry or lost agent ownership aborts the scan and restores the previous autosave state independently of the agent.

Restoring autosave cannot accidentally enable it when the owner deliberately had it disabled, or send cleanup commands to a newly started process. An adapter reports the prior state where possible; otherwise online backup requires an explicitly configured/acknowledged autosave baseline.

If the selected process adapter cannot provide this cleanup guarantee, Vesta explains the limitation and offers stopped-server backup instead. After host restart, journals are reconciled before launching or resuming operations.
VSS or other snapshot privileges are isolated to a narrowly scoped local helper; enabling snapshot support does not make the public agent an OS admin.
Schedules execute locally without a launcher connection.
The scheduler is a durable typed workflow engine, not only a cron/action list. Workflows compose built-in steps and locally installed script presets in an owner-defined order.

Steps have typed inputs and outputs. Workflows may add delays, pass outputs to later steps, branch on success/failure or validated output conditions, and set retries, timeouts, and failure behavior. Example: create backup; on success, clean trash; then emit a notification.
Scheduled actions, workflow state, outputs, retries, and failures are durable and auditable across agent restarts.

Notifications are stored locally and track read/acknowledged state per Vesta principal, with delivery cursors so any of that principal's devices can fetch events missed while offline without creating separate notification accounts.
External delivery integrations are optional and must not be required for core operation.

Built-in steps include backup, backup verification, start/stop/restart, console command, delay, update check/install, trash cleanup, notification, and local script preset. Notification is a real workflow action with selected destinations and severity.

Arbitrary remote script authoring is not exposed. Scripts/hooks are installed locally as server-side presets; launcher users with permission may select a preset and allowed parameters when creating a schedule.
Script presets run under the server's unprivileged identity with fixed working directories, environment allowlists, timeouts, output limits, parameter validation, and an auditable content hash.
Preset definitions can be reloaded without restarting the agent after schema, path, ownership, and security validation.
Initial workflows are sequential with conditional branches and no loops or parallel branches.

Triggers include manual, calendar/cron, fixed interval, agent startup, server start/stop/crash, first-player-join, last-player-leave/player-count-zero, update available, backup completion/failure, and resource thresholds.
Backup schedules and retention are opt-in and configurable. Presets may include minimal daily retention and daily/weekly/monthly policies.
Minecraft log rotation/cleanup is independently configurable by age, total size, and free-space policy.

Each workflow has an execution principal. Current role, resource scope, credential/grant expiry, and preset approval are checked before each mutating step, not only at schedule creation. Revoked authority suspends affected work and creates an audit event/notification; schedules cannot preserve old access.

Missed schedule occurrences have an explicit policy: skip and notify, run the latest eligible occurrence, or bounded catch-up. Dangerous/non-idempotent work is never inferred from historical console lines or blindly repeated. The confirmed default is skip-and-notify, configurable per workflow. Reconciliation of notifications, process state, and already-started operations is separate and still occurs after recovery.

Every long-running or materially mutating action is represented by a durable operation with an identifier, actor, requested inputs, lifecycle state, timestamps, progress, safe-to-cancel state, result/error, and audit correlation.
Operations include backups, verification, restore, updates, Vesta Pack builds, archive work, large file transactions, imports/exports, lifecycle transitions, diagnostics, and maintenance workflows.
A persistent task queue survives launcher disconnection and agent restart. Authorized clients can subscribe to progress or reconnect and retrieve it.

Named resource locks serialize conflicting work. Conflicts normally queue in request order; harmless redundant lifecycle requests may be coalesced or rejected with the existing operation identifier. Local recovery work has a controlled priority path.

Restore, agent activation, pack publication, and other destructive transitions are exclusive against operations that could observe or alter inconsistent state. Read-only work may continue concurrently when its inputs are stable.

Cancellation occurs only at declared safe points. If an operation cannot be safely cancelled, the API explains why and completes or rolls back the current transaction instead of abruptly terminating it.

Stop and force-kill requests may receive queue priority, but never silently interrupt consistency-sensitive work. If a backup or comparable operation is active, the client must explicitly confirm cancellation of that exact operation before the kill proceeds; cleanup and operation state remain auditable.

After process or machine failure, idempotent/safe work may resume or retry. Interrupted destructive work uses its journal to roll back or enters an explicit `recovery_required` state; it is never blindly replayed.

Completed operation summaries default to 90-day retention. Retention duration, bounded task output, and total task-history storage are configurable; security facts required by audit policy remain independently retained.
Raw Minecraft stdin executes with console authority and has no native remote user identity. Vesta therefore authorizes commands before writing to stdin.

Vesta does not require owners to design a Minecraft command-policy language. Moderator-oriented operations use dedicated typed actions and safe built-in presets rather than unrestricted console strings.
Administrators/Maintainers with explicit raw-console capability may use full console. A Moderator has no raw-console entry by default.

Vesta does not provide `execute_as_player`. Platform inconsistencies and online-player requirements make it unreliable; dedicated moderation actions and explicit full-console permission are the supported boundaries.

The player-management baseline includes online players, kick, temporary and permanent ban with reason, pardon, whitelist add/remove, OP/de-OP and OP level, kill, lightning strike, and auditable history.
IP bans, mute, teleport, and inventory inspection are plugin/connector extensions unless later promoted to core actions.
Console and log output is not heuristically redacted. Access is restricted to explicit log/console capabilities and all access is audited.
Live console history is an in-memory 10,000-line ring buffer only. Vesta does not duplicate persistent console history because Minecraft already writes its own logs.

The supervisor continuously drains stdout/stderr even without a viewer, so a full process pipe cannot stall Minecraft. The bounded buffer may include early JVM failures not present in game logs; this is not another persistent log store.

Catch-up reads Minecraft's existing logs using file identity/offset cursors, with rotation/truncation handling and bounded scans of retained archives. Missing/deleted logs produce a visible history gap, not fabricated events or replay of commands. Connector/status reconciliation corrects uncertain player state before sleep or player-dependent automation resumes.
Vesta retains its own bounded operational diagnostics and required security audit records; these describe Vesta actions, not a duplicate Minecraft log.
Player join/leave history and aggregate activity are retained as metrics under the configured metrics retention policy.
Sandboxing is optional but recommended.
Docker is not the only isolation option and is not required on Windows.

Baseline isolation uses a dedicated unprivileged OS identity, strict filesystem ACLs, process-tree ownership, resource limits, and network policy. Secure service setup uses distinct identities for the game and control plane; containers and stronger sandboxing remain optional additions.
Hardened Linux profiles may add systemd sandboxing, namespaces/cgroups, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, or rootless containers.
Hardened Windows profiles may add a restricted service identity, directory ACLs, Job Objects, and Windows Firewall rules.
One Java runtime is configured for the single server instance. Setup detects or installs a compatible Java version, and the owner may override it with a custom executable path.
Runtime compatibility is validated before server installation, update, or launch.
Setup may download and manage one signed compatible runtime distribution, with a user-supplied Java executable as an alternative.

"One runtime" means the configured game runtime. If Vesta itself needs a different runtime, it is bundled/managed independently by the one installer; old Minecraft Java requirements must not force an obsolete agent runtime.

Minecraft 1.7+ is a protocol/process compatibility target, not a promise that every optional connector, metric, loader, or online-backup command works on every version. The tested adapter matrix and capability discovery say exactly what is supported; unsupported features have an honest fallback.
Raw operational samples are retained for 24 hours at approximately ten-second resolution.
Five-minute aggregates are retained for 30 days.
Daily summaries are retained for one year.
Retention and total metrics storage have configurable ceilings and cleanup is performed locally.

Configuration may set Java memory, process priority, CPU affinity where supported, and disk warning/critical thresholds. Strong cgroup/Job Object limits are available only on platforms and isolation profiles that support them.
The agent can refuse storage-expanding operations below a configurable critical free-space threshold while preserving owner recovery and cleanup operations.
Critical-disk actions are configurable. Notification/refusal is the safe default; an owner may explicitly configure a workflow such as backup cleanup or server stop.

A configurable low-disk policy may delete expired staging/temp files and expired trash, then prune only backup snapshots already eligible under the active retention policy. It never silently removes unexpired backups or live server data. Cleanup order, thresholds, and automatic execution are visible and configurable.

An authorized user can generate and download a diagnostic bundle containing agent logs, Minecraft logs/crash reports, version/environment data, recent metrics, and configuration with known credentials and protected secrets removed.
There is no automatic third-party log-upload integration in the baseline; diagnostic and log export is manual.
Setup recommends Java memory from available host RAM and detected server type, while allowing owner override.
The wrapper remains fully useful with a vanilla server and no connector.

Loader mods/plugins are optional capability adapters for accurate player events, TPS/MSPT and tick health, coordinated world flushes, join enforcement, native whitelist/ban operations, and other in-process signals.

The connector is not an administrative authority. Because it shares a process with third-party server code, a compromised mod/plugin environment must not be able to grant wrapper roles, access files, rotate credentials, or approve updates.

The no-connector baseline relies on documented server commands, console/log parsing, status probes, and file inspection. Parsers are versioned adapters and surface uncertainty instead of inventing player or health state.
Direct authenticated HTTPS remains the mandatory self-hosted transport.
The endpoint accepts DNS hostnames such as `play.example.net` as well as IPv4 and IPv6 literals. IPv4 and IPv6 have first-class bind, advertise, firewall, certificate, and diagnostic handling.

Entering a Minecraft address can discover the Vesta API through a `_vesta._tcp` DNS SRV record. A configurable HTTPS `/.well-known/vesta-server` descriptor is a secondary discovery path, and complete manual API URL entry is always supported.

A compatible connector may advertise the same endpoint/server-ID hint in an extended Minecraft status response while the server is live; Vesta's offline status responder emits it while sleeping/offline. Discovery hints are untrusted until certificate/server identity and pairing are verified.

Vesta serves no browser-based management panel. HTTPS exists for the launcher, public status, pack distribution, and third-party protocol clients; local bootstrap/recovery remains available through the wrapper CLI.
One configurable HTTPS listener normally serves public status, pack, and authenticated management routes with per-route authorization. Optional SFTP remains a separate protocol/port.
Initial operation may use LAN access, explicit port forwarding, a user-managed VPN/overlay, or a reverse proxy.

A bring-your-own, self-hosted end-to-end encrypted relay is a later CGNAT feature rather than a dependency of the direct-connect release. It requires a publicly reachable owner-operated host; no Vesta-operated relay is mandatory.
Relay transport, if implemented, must not be able to decrypt management traffic or impersonate either endpoint.

The first networking implementation uses direct HTTPS plus diagnostics for LAN reachability, firewall rules, public addressing, and port forwarding. Automatic UPnP/NAT-PMP mapping is never enabled without explicit owner consent.

Setup may create host firewall rules after explicit confirmation and verifies local bind/listener/firewall state. End-to-end public reachability is tested by a paired launcher on another network or an optional stateless external probe; core operation never depends on a Vesta-operated checking service.

The agent advertises one canonical public endpoint. Launchers may manually retain LAN/VPN alternatives, but automatic multi-address priority/failover is deferred until a concrete need justifies its complexity.

Optional LAN mDNS discovery may advertise a safe server ID/name and endpoint, but is a low-priority, onboarding-configurable convenience distinct from normal DNS hostname entry and reveals no credentials.

A trusted reverse-proxy mode supports owner-operated HTTP proxies that terminate public TLS. Device-key proof remains application-layer authenticated, proxy source addresses are explicitly trusted, forwarded client-address headers are accepted only from those sources, and the origin hop is authenticated.
Direct and TCP-passthrough deployments retain end-to-end mutual TLS. Reverse proxy termination does not silently downgrade into bearer-token-only access.
Access modes are composable, not mutually exclusive presets. A reverse-proxy deployment can keep loopback/LAN management available while also exposing its configured public routes through the proxy.

Onboarding can optionally detect a local Nginx/Caddy/Traefik installation, generate a reviewed Vesta site/upstream configuration, back up any touched configuration, validate it with the proxy's native checker, and reload only after success. It never silently installs or rewrites an unrelated proxy.

Optional ACME certificate issuance/renewal supports owners with a domain. A locally generated pinned certificate remains the universal default, and ACME failure cannot remove CLI recovery or silently replace server identity.

ACME HTTP-01 requires reachable port 80 and TLS-ALPN-01 requires port 443; neither automatically works merely because Vesta's chosen API port is open. Onboarding detects conflicts/exposure and recommends proxy-managed certificates or an owner-supplied DNS-validated certificate when direct validation cannot work. No DNS-provider secret is required for normal local/pinned setup.

Direct deployments initially automate HTTP-01/TLS-ALPN ACME validation. Reverse-proxy deployments normally let the proxy own ACME. DNS-01 uses an owner-supplied ACME client/certificate path initially; provider-specific DNS credential integrations are deferred.

Route exposure is independently configurable. Remote management may be disabled or limited to loopback/LAN while public status and authorized pack downloads continue. Roles still govern access whenever management is exposed.
Disabling remote management immediately rejects new remote requests and closes existing remote management event/session channels; loopback CLI recovery is unaffected.

Changing the advertised hostname may preserve pairings when continuity of the same server identity is proven. Launchers still require low-priority endpoint approval before sending management requests to the new address.
Limited Minecraft-style public status remains available even when pack access is password-gated or Minecraft-policy-gated.
Management and SFTP support configurable IP/CIDR allow and deny rules as an additional condition after identity authentication.

Minecraft `banned-ips.json` remains a game-admission source, not the canonical management firewall. Owners may explicitly enable inheritance of its denied addresses into pack/management/SFTP network policy; independent Vesta rules remain available to avoid accidental owner lockout or shared-NAT surprises.
Management HTTPS uses mutual TLS. The agent presents its pinned server identity and each paired device has a server-scoped client certificate bound to its principal/device record.
Public-CA certificates are supported for server transport identity without replacing per-device client authentication.

The stable Vesta identity key is distinct from a renewable HTTPS certificate. Public-CA certificate renewal with valid hostname/chain and the same verified Vesta identity does not require pairing again. Locally pinned transport keys and the stable identity key have explicit authenticated rotation/continuity flows. An unexpected identity change or unproven pinned-key rotation blocks management until verified locally/out-of-band; failed TLS validation is not silently ignored. Public unauthenticated status may still be displayed with a prominent unverified-identity warning.

Public status, discovery, and pairing must remain reachable without an existing client certificate. Listener/proxy configuration distinguishes these routes while every management route requires verified device authentication; an absent client certificate cannot downgrade management into unauthenticated access.
Optional TOTP or a local security PIN provides configurable step-up authentication for selected sensitive operations. It is disabled by default.
Local recovery requires OS-level authorization: elevation on Windows and root or the dedicated Vesta service identity on Linux.
The agent provides an optional built-in SFTP service rooted in the Minecraft server directory for use with standard tools such as WinSCP and FileZilla.
SFTP is disabled until explicitly enabled during owner onboarding or later configuration.
SFTP and HTTPS file management share the same canonical file permissions, browser-ignore rules, protected internal paths, quotas, trash behavior, and audit events.

Authentication prefers per-principal SSH public keys. Password credentials, if enabled, are separately generated/revocable and use the same role-derived file capabilities; management or pack passwords are never reused directly.

A Vesta administrator uses the same local Vesta principal and role for SFTP, but registers a dedicated SSH public key or receives a separately revocable SFTP password. SFTP does not create an unrelated authorization database.

The canonical SFTP username is the stable Vesta principal UUID. A linked Minecraft UUID may be accepted as an alias. Credential expiry is configurable; SSH keys and generated passwords can have different lifetimes.

SFTP distinguishes list, read/download, create/upload, overwrite, rename, mkdir, and delete permissions. It prevents path/symlink escape, limits sessions and transfer rates, and logs authentication and file operations.

SFTP writes use standard live-file semantics. During overwrite, the original may be moved into recoverable trash first, but the new target is visible as it is uploaded; interrupted transfers can leave a partial file and a recoverable previous version.
SFTP and HTTPS file management support ZIP/TAR/GZIP archive creation and extraction with traversal, symlink, file-count, compression-ratio, expanded size, timeout, and disk-space protections.
Remote ownership changes are blocked. Safe permission-bit changes are configurable on supported Unix filesystems and have no fabricated equivalent on Windows.
The server SSH host key is generated locally, displayed during setup, and can be pinned by clients. SFTP listens on a separately configurable port.

Vesta minimizes credential sprawl by keeping one canonical principal and role assignment. Protocol credentials are authentication methods on that principal, not separate users, and each method can be listed, expired, rotated, or revoked independently from one place.

Device private keys remain on the launcher device. The server stores only the public key/certificate and revocation metadata. Human-entered passwords and recovery passphrases are stored only as Argon2id verifiers when decryption is not required.

Secrets that must be recovered in plaintext, such as Discord tokens, webhook credentials, SMTP credentials, and backup repository keys, live in an encrypted agent vault whose wrapping key is protected by the operating system. Windows uses service-identity/DPAPI protection; Linux uses service-only file permissions with an optional system keyring or TPM-backed key where available.
Secrets never appear in normal configuration export, file browsing, metrics, notifications, task output, or diagnostic bundles. Replacement is supported without revealing the current value.

Public status and pack endpoints have configurable per-IP and per-principal bandwidth, request-rate, concurrent-transfer, archive, and daily-transfer limits. Secure presets are enabled by default, including limits for anonymous clients.

Management HTTPS and SFTP apply configurable request/body/transfer limits, connection and session caps, authentication backoff, temporary IP throttling, and per-principal storage/transfer quotas. Local recovery cannot be blocked by remote throttling or network deny rules.

The management API provides schema-backed editors for `server.properties`, EULA state, JVM/memory settings, whitelist, bans, and recognized loader/server configuration while preserving raw text editing for authorized users.
Vesta validates structured edits, writes atomically, preserves formatting when practical, and reports whether a reload or restart may be needed.

Locally installed declarative schema extensions may add structured editors for server implementations and plugin/mod configuration. Raw text editing remains available, and schemas do not gain arbitrary agent code execution.
Provisioning or managing MySQL/PostgreSQL databases is out of scope. Vesta may protect database credentials found in server files but does not own external database lifecycle.

Owners can export normal configuration for portability and an encrypted full recovery package containing roles, device registrations, schedules, integrations, SFTP registrations, notification policy, and audit metadata.
Recovery export is distinct from the redacted diagnostic bundle. Secret-bearing recovery packages require owner authorization, strong encryption, and a separately preserved recovery key/passphrase.

Local durable state uses SQLite in WAL mode with foreign keys, versioned migrations, startup integrity checks, and a protected pre-migration snapshot. Database maintenance and snapshots participate in the operation queue.

The SQLite state directory stays on a supported local filesystem, not a network share used for backups. Live database exports use SQLite's supported backup mechanism, not an inconsistent copy of the database/WAL files.
Desired configuration and effective runtime state are tracked separately. Each changed setting declares whether it applies live, on agent restart, on Minecraft reload, or on Minecraft restart.

The API exposes a compact pending-change summary, affected settings, required action, and validation errors. A launcher can render this persistently, such as in a status control at the bottom of its navigation sidebar.

Roles, limits, notification routes, and schedules normally apply live. Listener/TLS/service changes require an agent restart; JVM, loader, and most Minecraft configuration changes report the appropriate reload/restart need.

Breaking state corruption prevents Minecraft launch by default and Vesta does not expose normal remote management against uncertain authorization data and enters a local recovery-required mode. The owner may configure a narrowly defined availability policy for non-security-critical failures, but corrupted identity, authorization, path, or launch-integrity state always fails closed.
Repair, restore, reset, or locally approved continuation requires an OS-authorized local confirmation and produces a permanent audit event.
Automatic service-level restart of the Vesta agent after an agent crash is an owner-configurable watchdog toggle. It is independent of the Minecraft start-on-agent-start and crash-restart policies.
Update channels are `stable`, `beta`, and `nightly`; `stable` is the default.
The agent checks for updates at startup and approximately every 24 hours.
Checks and optional staging may be automated, but installation, agent restart, and Minecraft restart always require explicit authorization.
Updates are signed, rollback-protected, staged, health-checked after activation, and retain the previous working agent version for recovery.

Recovery of an interrupted, uncommitted file transaction is distinct from restoring a backup after a completed but unhealthy update. Vesta reconciles journals to a known transaction state; it never silently restores worlds or chooses an older pack/server state after a health check fails. Agent-binary fallback must preserve state compatibility and report exactly what happened.

The default installation path is an interactive Windows PowerShell or Linux shell walkthrough. It supports choosing a new/existing server directory, process mode, Java runtime, service/portable operation, ports/firewall, TLS, initial owner pairing, pack policy, optional connector, start/restart policy, backups, update channel, and hardening profile.

The normal walkthrough asks only for a new/existing server, its detected or chosen implementation/version, intended access (local/LAN/internet), initial owner pairing, and opt-in features such as backups or a supported connector. Recommended settings are displayed together; advanced options expand only when requested. Owners are not required to understand IPC, TLS internals, script definitions, resource-limit primitives, or backup cryptography.

Network onboarding offers composable Local, LAN, Direct internet, Reverse proxy, and VPN/overlay choices rather than forcing one exclusive topology. It configures only the selected listeners/routes and explains the exposure.
Optional external port/reachability testing discloses that the public address is sent to a remote probe. Owners may instead complete an end-to-end test from a paired launcher on another network.
System-service operation is recommended and starts the agent with the machine. Portable/manual operation and integration with an existing Windows service or systemd unit are also supported.
Advanced/headless installations support documented non-interactive flags or an answer file using the same validation and backup acknowledgements.

Uninstallation is a guided set of explicit choices. Removing the Vesta service does not implicitly delete the Minecraft server, Vesta state, downloaded Java, backups, or recovery material; each removable data class is selected and described separately.
Audit records are tamper-evident, locally durable, and exportable as structured JSON.

Local tamper evidence is not protection against an OS administrator replacing the whole history. Optional external checkpoints/export can strengthen that guarantee without becoming a core service dependency.

Each event records the principal, authentication method/device, source address, operation, target, outcome, timestamp, and correlation/operation identifier. Sensitive changes include safe before/after hashes or redacted summaries, not raw file contents, credentials, tokens, or command output containing secrets.

General audit events have 180-day default retention. Security, ownership, credential, and recovery events are retained permanently unless removed by a local owner recovery operation with an audit export/warning.

Protected audit growth has storage monitoring, reserved capacity, and explicit local export/archival guidance. Vesta never silently prunes protected history or continues unaudited sensitive mutations when durable recording has failed.
Discord is an optional outbound integration for notifications, status presence, and read-only slash commands such as uptime, online count, and safe server status.

Optional Discord OAuth identity linking may associate a Discord user or guild role with a Vesta principal/role. Local Vesta authorization remains canonical, and Discord cannot grant Owner or Administrator authority.
Guild, channel, user, and role allowlists constrain bot output. Bot and webhook tokens are protected agent secrets and never exposed through normal file APIs.

Discord channels, visibility, slash commands, status presentation, event routes, Vesta role mappings, and whether supported actions are enabled are all owner-configurable. Presets provide a useful setup without hard-coding a community's access policy.
Vesta ships secure, useful presets and an interactive setup path so an owner does not need to design policies from scratch.

Presets are schema-backed configuration, not product lock-ins. Owners can customize roles, capabilities, pack rules, schedules, retention, notifications, Discord behavior, process policy, storage, network endpoints, and adapters.
Presets can be reset, exported, imported, and diffed against current settings.

Security invariants remain enforced even when surrounding policy is configurable: path confinement, protected agent secrets, authenticated local owner recovery, cryptographic verification, request limits, and auditable authorization cannot be disabled through ordinary remote configuration.
Velocity can be treated as a supported Java server process without requiring multi-server orchestration in the first release.
Proxy topology, forwarding secrets, backend network isolation, dependency ordering, and community-wide orchestration are later capabilities.

The management protocol is public and versioned: an OpenAPI-described HTTPS request API plus a versioned WebSocket or Server-Sent Events stream for task, console, status, metric, player, and notification events.

Compatibility negotiation, stable error codes, idempotency keys for mutating requests, pagination, event cursors, and deprecation windows are part of the protocol contract so third-party panels can be reliable clients.

Hosting-provider service principals are a niche optional deployment feature, disabled by default. If enabled, they receive explicitly configured scopes and server access and cannot silently obtain or delegate local Owner authority.

The initial complete release supports declarative configuration schemas, connector capability adapters, outbound webhooks, and locally installed script presets. These cover likely integrations without loading arbitrary third-party code into the privileged agent process.

A general in-process plugin API is deferred until concrete extension needs and a secure isolation/signing model exist. Future extensions must declare their capabilities, resources, compatibility, and trust source.

Product telemetry is completely disabled by default and core operation never depends on it. Owners may explicitly opt into a documented anonymous diagnostic dataset, preview exactly what is sent, and revoke consent at any time.
Argon2id for Vesta-owned human password verification. Mature backup engines retain their reviewed native key derivation rather than changing their format.
Device public-key authentication and short-lived sessions.
Per-device and per-principal revocation.
Strict TLS identity/pinning and certificate rotation.
Fine-grained authorization with deny-by-default policy.
Request/body/concurrency/storage limits and abuse controls.
Safe path resolution, protected internal roots, atomic writes, and operation transactions.
Append-only audit events for every authentication, authorization, console, file, content, backup, schedule, settings, update, and power operation.
Secret redaction, protected local storage, and platform-specific permissions.
Signed update metadata and rollback protection.
Threat-model and security regression tests before public release.
